title: Benji and the Falling Seeds
markdown:
Benji watched Dapple prance after a butterfly. “Ms. Quill!” he called. “Why did Dapple’s apple core drift down so slowly, like a puff? When I kicked a stone — zoom — it shot straight down. They’re both just falling, aren’t they?”

Dapple nodded, ears twitching, as if the butterfly had been part of the experiment and had simply refused to land.

Ms. Quill, eyes bright, chuckled. “A proper question. Come on.”

They ambled to a grassy hill. She took two sheets of paper, creased one into a sharp dart, the other into a wide glider. Benji gathered small dry seed pods, some with papery wings still attached, some as plain as pebbles.

“Ready?” from the crest. “One. Two. Three.”

The dart zipped. The glider wobbled and dipped. Benji’s winged seed took its sweet time. The plain seed dropped without manners.

Benji’s brow furrowed. “The air is pushing back.” He watched the glider drift, then land as if it had changed its mind twice.

“When something falls, the air tries to slow it. Wider and flatter, more air it bumps into. A sort of hug, if hugs were invisible and everywhere.”

Benji picked up a leaf. It caught the air and drifted. A twig fell faster, businesslike. A gust lifted a feather and sent it twirling high. “Look!” Dapple whinnied. “The feather dances!”

“It catches so much air. A tiny parachute.”

Benji’s eyes lit. His friend Pip was growing giant sunflower seeds. Benji needed to deliver them, and the meadow could be windy. Lost seeds would mean an empty gate and a long apology.

“If I make the packet wide and flat, like the glider, won’t it just float away?”

“It might. Pointed, like the dart, it cuts through. The wind has less to grab.”

Benji found bark and folded a neat pointed packet. The sunflower seeds went inside, counted twice. Dapple watched, ears perked, and did not try to eat the experiment.

“Ready?” Benji grinned. Dapple nudged his hand. He tossed. The packet sailed across the meadow in a steady line and landed at Pip’s garden gate, not in the hedge, not in the ditch.

“Hooray!” He hugged Dapple. The seeds were safe. Pip’s sunflowers, somewhere behind the gate, would not have to wait on the wind’s mood.

Ms. Quill smiled and named the push once, without making it a secret game: air resistance. Shape changed the fall. Benji looked at the sky, then at Dapple, who was already eyeing a dandelion — wide, flat, and entirely likely to dance.
